data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference is indefensible on Popper's own terms and constitutes a performative contradiction: when Popper chooses a well-corroborated bridge design, he acts exactly as an inductivist would, relying on the implicit premise that past survival indicates future stability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"refuted if it can be demonstrated that Popper explicitly justified the preference for better-corroborated theories in practical decisions solely on the grounds of maximizing testability and information content, without invoking any expectation of future success","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"refuted if a definitive textual analysis shows Popper distinguished 'rational preference' based on critical scrutiny from 'inductive inference'","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"refuted if Popper's later work on verisimilitude successfully decouples the preference for corroborated theories from any form of inductive logic","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"No amount of semantic maneuvering around 'corroboration' vs. 'probability' can mask the fact that acting on corroboration requires an inductive leap. Popper's system collapses into crypto-induction whenever it leaves the realm of abstract methodology, as the practical necessity of success forces the adoption of the very principle (uniformity of nature) he sought to destroy.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
